input:
It is important to note that phase equilibrium is a truly fundamental concept in thermodynamics, and understanding what happens when a pure component reaches its boiling point provides a foundation for many separation processes. At the boiling point, the liquid and vapour phases coexist in a state of balance, meaning that molecules pass from liquid into vapour while others return from vapour into liquid, the two opposing flows cancelling out. The system settles into a dynamic equilibrium in which the composition of each phase remains completely unchanged over time, provided that both phases are still present.

The formal condition that captures this state can be expressed in words, before any equation is introduced, as follows: equilibrium holds when the chemical potential of the component is the same in both phases. Chemical potential can be thought of as a measure of how strongly a component tends to escape from the phase it currently occupies. If the chemical potential in the liquid is higher than that in the vapour, molecules will tend to move from liquid to vapour and boiling will proceed; if it is lower, vapour will tend to condense back into liquid. Only when the two values are exactly equal does net transfer come to a halt, highlighting the central role that this equality plays in defining the boiling point itself.

Pressure also plays a significant role in this picture. Raising the pressure means that the vapour has to be compressed further before its chemical potential can rise to match that of the liquid, so equality is reached only at a higher temperature, whereas lowering the pressure allows equality to be reached at a lower temperature instead. A boiling point is therefore never a fixed property of a substance in isolation, and it should always be reported together with the pressure at which it applies, underscoring the close interdependence of temperature and pressure in phase behaviour.

Finally, it is worth emphasising that boiling a pure component does not change the composition of either phase, since each phase contains one and the same component. Boiling can change the relative amounts of liquid and vapour present, but it cannot enrich or purify anything, which is why separation by boiling has nothing to gain from a pure component.
target:
Phase equilibrium for a pure component at its boiling point is the condition in which liquid and vapour coexist without net change: molecules leave the liquid and return to it at equal rates, and the composition of each phase stays constant while both phases remain present. The condition is stated in words before any equation is named: at equilibrium, the chemical potential of the component has the same value in the two phases. Equality of chemical potential across the phases is the equilibrium condition, and the boiling point is the temperature at which that equality holds for the liquid and vapour of the pure component at the given pressure.

Chemical potential measures the tendency of a component to leave the phase it occupies. Where the chemical potential in the liquid stands higher than in the vapour, transfer runs from liquid to vapour and boiling continues; where it stands lower, transfer runs the other way and vapour condenses. Net transfer stops only where the two values meet, and the meeting of the two values is what the boiling point records. Boiling is not a one-way release of vapour: both directions of transfer continue at equal rates.

Temperature and pressure fix where equality can hold for a pure component. At a higher pressure, equality is reached at a higher temperature, because the vapour must be compressed further before its chemical potential rises to meet that of the liquid. At a lower pressure, equality comes at a lower temperature. The boiling point is tied to the pressure imposed on the component, and a statement of a boiling point without its pressure is incomplete.

The condition also bounds what boiling can do to a pure component. Transfer between the phases changes how much liquid and vapour are present, and it changes neither phase's composition, because each phase holds the one component only. Purity is preserved through boiling, and separation by boiling has no purchase on a pure component. Equality of chemical potential is the whole content of equilibrium here: a balance of tendencies to transfer, struck at the temperature the pressure selects.
